request: explain the OSI model of networking

composition.story: Why does networking need seven OSI layers? Follow one message, “Hi,” from the Sender through the Signal path to the Receiver. Compare the recovered message with the original. Assume successful delivery; protocol examples illustrate responsibilities, not seven mandatory software modules.

aha.observation: The Receiver recovers the original message because the layers perform different jobs around the same application data.

parts.presentation: Approved card shell; explanation above experiment; ordered state rail carries progress, never elapsed time. Brief parameter-control budget: zero; navigation is separate.
Canonical protocol composition with fixed Sender, Signal path, and Receiver. Highlight one active region; no animation or full layer matrix.
Anchor beside the named active region; reserve readable label space. Identify the location and explain its current responsibility.
Show message evidence and bound status below the picture; wrap long values. Reference capture shows recovered, held until learner action.

controls.label: OSI journey
controls.presentation: Previous and Next; default index 0, bounds 0–7, increment 1. Keep boundary buttons named and disabled; support keyboard activation and visible focus.

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Restore the first state and all defaults. Support keyboard activation and visible focus; no automatic advancement.

states.label: 7 · Application
states.sentence: Sender: Application provides network services used by applications, such as sending an HTTP message.
states.why: OSI describes responsibilities; this example uses HTTP, TCP, IP, and Ethernet without assuming a perfect OSI mapping.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: Application message carrying “Hi”

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Application message ready; Next examines its representation.

states.label: 6 · Presentation
states.sentence: Sender: Presentation handles data representation, such as encoding text in UTF-8.
states.why: Both endpoints must interpret the representation consistently; encoding does not change the intended message.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: Application message with “Hi” encoded as UTF-8 text

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Representation agreed; Next examines conversation management.

states.label: 5 · Session
states.sentence: Sender: Session manages the dialogue, including establishing, coordinating, and ending conversations.
states.why: Internet applications may implement these responsibilities themselves; a separate session-layer header is not required.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: Same encoded application message, within a managed conversation

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Conversation context ready; Next examines end-to-end transport.

states.label: 4 · Transport
states.sentence: Sender: Transport provides process-to-process delivery; TCP adds ordering and retransmission for reliable transfer.
states.why: In this simplified example, TCP places the application message inside one segment and identifies the communicating processes using ports.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: TCP segment containing the application message

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Transport information added; Next examines delivery across networks.

states.label: 3 · Network
states.sentence: Sender: Network provides addressing and routing between networks; IP carries the TCP segment toward its destination.
states.why: IP addresses identify network endpoints; routers use destination addressing to select forwarding paths.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: IP packet containing the TCP segment

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Network information added; Next examines delivery over one link.

states.label: 2 · Data link
states.sentence: Sender: Data link packages the IP packet for one local link, using an Ethernet frame in this example.
states.why: Link delivery reaches the next interface; it is different from routing across an entire network path.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: Ethernet frame containing the IP packet

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Link information added; Next examines physical transmission.

states.label: 1 · Physical
states.sentence: Signal path: Physical carries encoded bits as electrical, optical, or radio signals.
states.why: The medium carries signals representing the frame, not the word “Hi” directly.

readouts.label: Original message
readouts.value: Hi

readouts.label: Current representation
readouts.value: Physical signals encoding the Ethernet frame

readouts.label: Status
readouts.value: Frame transmitted; Next compares the recovered message.

states.label: Receiver · Compare
states.sentence: Receiver: The receiving stack reverses encapsulation and delivers the recovered message to the application.
states.why: Different layers supplied different services around the same application data; the matching messages are the final evidence.

readouts.value: Hi

readouts.value: Hi
